title: How Anšar became a name the internet can speak
description: A scholarly look at Anšar, the primordial sky of Babylonian cosmogony, and the fight to keep original names on the web.
author: PuniCodex Team
body:
# How Anšar became a name the internet can speak

Saying **Anšar** aloud is harder than reading it on a screen, and more rewarding. The restored spelling is a compressed pronunciation guide: the caron above the s tells the reader to make a sound like the sh in 'ship'. That small mark — the difference between Anšar and Anshar — is the difference between a standard Assyriological transliteration and a flattened ASCII approximation. This post unpacks those instructions and then zooms out to the full record around the name: its Cuneiform writing, its role in the Babylonian creation epic Enūma Eliš, its pairing with Kišar, and its modern life as a Unicode domain.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Anšar
- **ASCII form:** anshar
- **Meaning:** 'Whole sky'
- **Domain of influence:** Sky, Circle of Heaven, Primordial Cosmos
- **Pantheon:** Mesopotamian
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** 𒀭𒀭𒊹 (Cuneiform)
- **Live domain:** none — this is a domainless flagship

## Overview

**Anšar** is the primordial sky of Babylonian cosmogony, the 'Whole Heaven' that arises from the mingling of the primordial waters Apsû and Tiāmat. With his consort Kišar, the Whole Earth, he forms the second generation of gods, the parents of Anu, and the ancestors of the great divine assembly. He is less a personal god than a cosmic principle: the upper half of the created order, the vast dome that contains the stars, the winds, and the gods themselves.

The name is written 𒀭𒀭𒊹 in cuneiform. The first sign, 𒀭, is the divine determinative; the following signs read An-šar. The etymology is Akkadian: *an* 'heaven' + *šar* 'totality, whole'. The Unicode restoration **Anšar** recovers the standard Assyriological transliteration. Because it preserves the postalveolar fricative š, the entry is classed Tier 1.

## The Name

The name **Anšar** appears in cuneiform as 𒀭𒀭𒊹 in the Babylonian creation epic Enūma Eliš. The etymology is clear: Akkadian *an* means 'heaven' and *šar* means 'totality' or 'whole', giving 'Whole Sky' or 'Totality of Heaven'. The name forms a natural pair with **Kišar**, whose name combines *ki* 'earth' with the same *šar* 'totality', giving 'Whole Earth'.

The ASCII form *anshar* flattens the distinctive š consonant to the digraph sh. This may seem like a minor change, but it erases a phonemic distinction. In Assyriological convention, š represents the voiceless postalveolar fricative /ʃ/, a single sound written with one letter. The digraph sh suggests two sounds and does not correspond to standard scholarly practice. A reader who knows Akkadian cannot recover the proper transliteration from *anshar* alone. The restoration **Anšar** removes that ambiguity and places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation is instructive: the initial *a* is capitalised, the *n* stays the same, the *sh* digraph becomes the single letter **š**, and the final *ar* stays the same. That single change — sh to š — is enough to restore a distinctive phoneme and a standard scholarly convention.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of Anšar is **/anˈʃaːr/** in Akkadian terms. The first syllable is light, the second carries the main stress, and the *a* of the second syllable is long. The *š* is the voiceless postalveolar fricative, like the sh in English 'ship'. The final *r* is a tapped consonant. For English-speaking readers, the closest approximation is 'ahn-SHAR' — stress the second syllable and let the sh sound crisp.

As with all Akkadian names, this pronunciation is a scholarly reconstruction. The cuneiform writing system represents consonants and vowels syllabically, and the actual phonetics may have varied by period and dialect. What matters for the Unicode restoration is that š is the standard scholarly symbol for this sound, and its presence in the name carries information that the digraph sh cannot.

## Original Script and Scholarly Transliteration

The name is preserved in Sumero-Akkadian cuneiform as **𒀭𒀭𒊹**. Cuneiform is one of the world's earliest writing systems, produced by pressing a reed stylus into wet clay. It was used across Mesopotamia from the fourth millennium BCE until the early Common Era and remained the medium for the great mythological and religious texts of the region.

For Anšar, the cuneiform consists of the divine determinative 𒀭 followed by signs read An-šar. This is the original script in which the name was attested. The Unicode restoration **Anšar** is the standard scholarly transliteration of that cuneiform writing. The cuneiform form itself is not registrable in the .com IDN table, which is why PuniCodex uses the Latin transliteration as the canonical domain form.

The label 'Original Script and Scholarly Transliteration' is therefore appropriate: the cuneiform is the attested writing, and Anšar is the scholarly reading that preserves a phonemic distinction and a scholarly convention lost in plain ASCII.

## The Mythology

Anšar's mythology is concentrated in the Babylonian creation epic Enūma Eliš. He is one of the primordial gods who arise from the first waters, the father of Anu, and the ancestor from whom Marduk will eventually spring. His role is cosmogonic rather than narrative: he names the structure of the world before the world has heroes.

The epic begins before heaven and earth existed, when only **Apsû** the sweet waters and **Tiāmat** the salt waters were mingled together. Their waters produced **Lahmu** and **Lahamu**, the silt deposits at the edge of the waters, and these in turn produced **Anšar** and **Kišar**, the Whole Sky and the Whole Earth. The pair thus represents the first cosmic differentiation into upper and lower, the fundamental binary on which the later cosmos is built.

Anšar and Kišar together beget **Anu**, the great sky god of later Mesopotamian religion. Anu in turn begets **Ea** (Enki), and Ea begets **Marduk**. Anšar therefore stands at the head of the divine genealogy that culminates in Marduk's kingship over the gods. When Tiāmat later raises an army of monsters to avenge Apsû's death, the younger gods are terrified. Anšar, as the eldest of the assembled gods, summons the divine council and eventually appoints Marduk as champion to face Tiāmat. His authority is that of the senior ancestor, the voice of cosmic order against chaos.

## Why Tier 1 Is the Right Classification

PuniCodex classifies names according to whether their Unicode restoration recovers distinctive information that the ASCII form loses. For Anšar, the restoration preserves the postalveolar fricative **š**, a phoneme that the ASCII digraph sh misrepresents.

The Tier 1 classification reflects this mechanical fact: the ASCII form *anshar* not only flattens the name visually but also misrepresents its scholarly transliteration. The digraph sh implies two consonants where the cuneiform and the standard reading give one. The restored **Anšar** removes that ambiguity. This is exactly the kind of information-rich restoration that Tier 1 is designed to recognise.

## Citation and Respect

Restoring **Anšar** as a flagship temple is an act of scholarly respect. It marks the name as a proper noun of continuing significance and situates it within the scholarly discourse of Assyriology. The ASCII form *anshar* is useful for domain names and search queries, but it carries none of the precision of the citation form.

At the same time, PuniCodex acknowledges that the cuneiform sources are only one layer of the figure's significance. The Enūma Eliš was recited and copied for more than a millennium, and its cosmological ideas influenced Mesopotamian religion and beyond. The restoration is offered as a starting point for that journey, not as the final word.

## The Meaning Behind the Name

The meaning of Anšar is clear: 'Whole Sky' or 'Totality of Heaven'. But the simplicity of the etymology opens onto deeper cosmological ideas. The *šar* element means totality or completeness; it is the same root that gives us the word for 'universe' or 'totality' in later Akkadian. To call the sky Anšar is not merely to name a region but to assert that the heavens are a complete, bounded whole.

The name also encodes a Babylonian way of thinking about the cosmos. The world is not an infinite expanse but a structured order: upper and lower, heaven and earth, each a totality in itself. Anšar is the upper totality, the complement and counterpart of Kišar's lower totality. Together they form the first cosmic pair, the foundation on which all later divine order rests.

## Mythology and Worldview

Anšar's mythology reflects a worldview in which the cosmos is created by differentiation. Before Anšar and Kišar, there were only waters; after them, there is heaven and earth. This is not creation ex nihilo but creation by separation and pairing. The gods do not make the world from nothing; they emerge from it and give it structure through their relationships.

This worldview has implications for how we understand Mesopotamian religion. The gods are not outside nature but arise from it. Heaven and earth are themselves divine or proto-divine, and the great gods of the pantheon are their descendants. Anšar's role as primordial sky is therefore not a mere backstory; it is the theological foundation for the entire pantheon.

## Cultural Significance Today

Anšar's legacy is literary and cosmological rather than cultic. The Enūma Eliš, in which he appears, was recited at the Babylonian New Year festival and shaped Mesopotamian ideas of cosmic order for more than a millennium. The pairing of Anšar and Kišar as heaven and earth is one of the earliest expressions of binary cosmology found across Eurasia, echoed in Greek Ouranos and Gaia, Chinese Tian and Di, and many other traditions.

In modern scholarship, Anšar serves as a key figure in discussions of Mesopotamian creation theology and the development of the Marduk cult. His name occasionally appears in fantasy and occult contexts as an archaic sky power. For students of comparative mythology, he is a reminder that the idea of a primordial heaven-earth pair is one of humanity's oldest ways of imagining the cosmos.

## Why This Restoration Matters

The restoration of **Anšar** matters because it resists the flattening of ancient names into generic lowercase strings. When a search engine or a domain registry displays *anshar*, it presents the name as data stripped of scholarly meaning. When it displays **Anšar**, it presents the name as a proper noun with a pronunciation, a cosmology, and a scholarly tradition behind it.

The internet was built on ASCII assumptions that privilege the Latin alphabet without diacritics and treat lowercase as the default. Those assumptions erase the phonemic distinctions and scholarly conventions of many languages and traditions. Restoring Anšar as a flagship temple is one small act of acknowledging that erasure and making space for scholarly and respectful forms online.

## A Note on Sources and Respect

The account of Anšar given here rests on the cuneiform textual record and on more than a century of Assyriological scholarship. The Enūma Eliš is available in Benjamin Foster's *Before the Muses* and in W. G. Lambert's *Babylonian Creation Myths*. Standard reference works such as Black and Green's *Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia* and the Chicago Assyrian Dictionary supply the iconographic and lexical context.

Readers who wish to learn more should consult these scholarly resources and the growing body of popularisations that engage critically with the ancient sources. The PuniCodex temple is offered as a starting point, not as the final word on a figure whose meanings continue to unfold.

## Related Names

The Mesopotamian pantheon holds many figures whose stories overlap or contrast with **Anšar**. His consort and complement is **Kišar**, the Whole Earth. Their son is **Anu**, the great sky god. **Apsû** and **Tiāmat** are the primordial waters from whom Anšar and Kišar arise. **Marduk**, the champion of the gods, is Anšar's great-grandson through Anu and Ea. Other primordial or cosmic figures include **Lahmu** and **Lahamu**, the silt deposits born of Apsû and Tiāmat.

For researchers and readers, the important distinction is between the scholarly citation form **Anšar** and the lowercase ASCII form *anshar*. The scholarly form preserves the š consonant and marks the name as a proper noun. The lowercase form is a technological artifact, useful for domain names and search queries but carrying none of the precision of the citation form.
